extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and counsel implementing Title IX grievance and supportive-measure policies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for providing, modifying, challenging, disclosing, and terminating supportive measures under 34 CFR §106.44(g) in Title IX proceedings, including distinctions from emergency removal and required procedures for impartial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must not unreasonably burden either party
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures must not unreasonably burden either the complainant or the respondent and must be designed to protect the safety of the parties or the recipient's educational environment or to provide support during grievance procedures or informal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department replaced earlier language to clarify that supportive measures can impose burdens on a party, but such burdens cannot be unreasonable. The unreasonableness determination must account for the nature of the educational programs, activities, opportunities, and benefits in which the party participates (not only academic components). Examples: stay-away orders or scheduling/class registration changes can be burdensome but permissible if not punitive and if they preserve access. Actions like suspension or expulsion are inherently burdensome and would be unreasonable supportive measures. The Department declined to provide an exhaustive list to preserve case-by-case flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must not be imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must not impose supportive measures for punitive or disciplinary reasons; supportive measures are intended to fulfill the purposes set forth in §106.2, not to punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule changed 'may' to 'must' to emphasize the prohibition. A punitive or disciplinary measure is one intended to punish conduct that violates Title IX; if a party can show a supportive measure was intended to punish (e.g., it does not remedy barriers to access), the recipient must terminate it. The fact that an action can be used later as a disciplinary sanction does not make it inherently disciplinary when used as a supportive measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-specific inquiry to determine whether a burden is reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are expected to engage in a fact-specific inquiry to determine whether supportive measures constitute a reasonable (or unreasonable) burden on a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inquiry should consider unique circumstances and the nature of the recipient's educational programs and activities. The Department will not define a single standard or exhaustive list of reasonable/unreasonable measures because flexibility is needed to account for facts and individual needs. For elementary and secondary settings, quick interventions (e.g., seating changes, educational conversations) are ordinarily reasonable supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both parties may be burdened but neither may be unreasonably burdened
rubrics_metrics.description: Both complainants and respondents may receive supportive measures that impose burdens, but the regulation prohibits unreasonably burdening either party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that supportive measures are not limited to mutual contact restrictions and that a recipient has discretion to provide individualized measures to restore or preserve access while preserving parties' rights. The rule seeks to avoid any implication that respondents are presumptively treated differently; burdens must be reasonable and non-punitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures are distinct from emergency removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing supportive measures is different from emergency removal; supportive measures do not require the individualized safety and risk analysis or the 'imminent and serious threat' threshold required for emergency removal under §106.44(h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency removal permits temporary removal when an individualized safety and risk analysis shows an imminent and serious threat. Supportive measures can be provided to restore or preserve access and protect safety without meeting that threshold; the Department declined to require the same safety and risk analysis for supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify or terminate supportive measures at the conclusion of grievance procedures when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient should, as appropriate, modify or terminate supportive measures at the conclusion of grievance procedures or the informal resolution process, though it may continue them beyond the conclusion when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must consider whether the measure continues to meet the definition of 'supportive measures' after procedures conclude. A determination of non-responsibility will often constitute materially changed circumstances requiring modification/termination. Parties may seek modification/termination based on materially changed circumstances under §106.44(g)(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures are not 'relevant evidence' for responsibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures should not be considered 'relevant evidence' in reaching a determination of responsibility under §106.45(b)(6) and (h)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explicitly states that providing supportive measures is distinct from evidence considered in adjudications and should not be used to infer responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely opportunity to challenge supportive measures by an appropriate and impartial employee (when applicable to the party)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complainant or respondent must have a timely opportunity to seek modification or reversal of the recipient's decision to provide, deny, modify, or terminate supportive measures from an appropriate and impartial employee when such measures are applicable to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.44(g)(4) requires independent review but gives recipients flexibility on timing and structure. The impartial reviewer may modify or reverse a decision when it is inconsistent with the definition of 'supportive measures.' The reviewer cannot be the same employee who provided the measure (no reviewer-provider conflict). The requirement is limited to measures 'applicable to' the party seeking review (e.g., a measure affecting only the complainant may not be challengeable by the respondent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases for challenging a supportive measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges may include whether a supportive measure is reasonably burdensome, reasonably available, imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons, imposed with a fee or charge, or effective in meeting its intended purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department added language clarifying that an impartial employee may reverse or modify a decision for these and other inconsistencies with the definition of 'supportive measures' in §106.2. Effectiveness (does it restore/preserve access, provide safety, or support during grievance procedures) is a basis for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and formality of challenges: recipients have flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have discretion regarding when a challenge opportunity must be provided; they are not required to provide an opportunity before imposition of a supportive measure and are not required to follow a formal fact-specific process to determine timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department deleted language implying a required formal 'fact-specific inquiry' about timeliness. A recipient may conduct informal inquiries consistent with the regulations. Mathews balancing principles justify allowing post-deprivation review where necessary. The recipient may set reasonable procedures consistent with timely independent review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial review assignment: avoid provider-reviewer conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure independent review, the employee who provides or denies supportive measures must not be permitted to also review challenges to the same supportive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title IX Coordinators may delegate provision/denial to another employee and serve as reviewer, or the Title IX Coordinator may designate an impartial administrator to review challenges; at minimum, one additional impartial person must be assigned to handle challenged decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality limits: disclosure of supportive measures restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about supportive measures must be maintained confidentially and disclosed only as necessary to restore or preserve a party's access or where exceptions apply; §106.44(g)(5) works with §106.44(j) (nondisclosure of personally identifiable information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section §106.44(g)(5) protects information about supportive measures beyond personally identifiable information covered by §106.44(j). Example: a respondent who knows the complainant's identity is not entitled to know that the complainant is receiving counseling services. §106.44(g)(5) permits disclosure when any exceptions in §106.44(j)(1)-(5) apply. Concerns about conflicts with FERPA and required disclosures to federal agencies were raised; the regulation ties into §106.44(j) to address such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients are not required to equalize supportive measures for both parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require recipients to apply every supportive measure equally to both complainant and respondent; supportive measures are intended to be individualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring equal application (e.g., providing both parties with identical escorts when only one needs it) would be inconsistent with individualized remedies and unduly burdensome. Recipients retain discretion to select measures necessary to restore/preserve access without blanket equality requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients are not required to proactively modify measures; parties may seek modification when ineffective or circumstances materially change
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not obliged to continuously monitor and affirmatively modify or initiate supportive measures; however, a party may seek modification or termination when a measure is ineffective or circumstances change materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to require proactive affirmative modification because of the burdens this would impose. §106.44(g)(4) provides the mechanism for parties to seek adjustments; materially changed circumstances vary by context (e.g., complainant withdraws from class or respondent found not responsible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures should be provided without fee or charge (challengeable if not)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a supportive measure is imposed without fee or charge is a permissible basis for challenge under §106.44(g)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department listed 'whether the supportive measure is being imposed without fee or charge' among the issues an impartial reviewer may consider. The implication is that charging a party for a supportive measure is inconsistent with the definition of 'supportive measures' and subject to reversal or modification.
